query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a nanoscale, conformal molybdenum (Mo) interlayer at the tungsten–copper interface during composite fabrication will reduce interfacial thermal resistance and boost overall thermal conductivity without degrading the mechanical durability or irradiation resistance of the composite.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu metal-matrix composite produced by standard consolidation methods, where discrete tungsten and copper phases contact each other with relatively high thermal boundary resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin Mo interlayer (via sputtering or chemical deposition) on the tungsten components prior to copper infiltration and composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: Processing under an inert atmosphere at temperatures sufficient for copper melt infiltration (but below tungsten’s melting point) and operating in application conditions typical of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint components (high thermal flux, mechanical stress, and neutron irradiation).
generation.structural_mediator: A coherent, nanoscale Mo layer at the W–Cu interface that promotes improved metallurgical bonding and lattice matching between tungsten and copper, thereby reducing the thermal interface resistance.
generation.mechanism: The Mo interlayer, chosen for its high thermal conductivity and excellent bonding properties, acts as an intermediary that mitigates the abrupt change in lattice structure and electronic density between tungsten and copper. This graded interface lowers thermal boundary resistance while Mo’s inherent mechanical strength and irradiation resilience help sustain the composite’s overall durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: An effective thermal conductivity increase on the order of approximately 10–20% compared to a standard W–Cu composite, with mechanical properties and irradiation resistance remaining comparable to the baseline material.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites fabricated without any engineered interfacial layer, exhibiting lower effective thermal conductivity due to higher interfacial thermal resistance.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to hold for composites operating under high heat flux, mechanical loading, and typical neutron irradiation levels found in fusion-reactor joint applications. However, excessive Mo thickness or suboptimal deposition conditions may lead to degradation, and the long-term stability under cyclical thermal/irradiation conditions remains to be confirmed.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the thermal conductivity enhancement and the long-term interfacial stability under prolonged neutron irradiation are uncertain and require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites under identical processing conditions. One set incorporates a nanoscale Mo interlayer on tungsten surfaces, and the other is produced by the standard method (control). Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling and neutron irradiation representative of fusion-reactor environments. Evaluate thermal conductivity, mechanical strength (e.g., tensile and impact tests), and interfacial integrity using microscopy techniques (TEM/SEM) before and after exposure.
measurements: Effective thermal conductivity (e.g., via laser flash analysis)
Microstructural characterization of the interface (TEM/SEM, EDS)
Irradiation damage assessment (neutron fluence, defect density)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-interlayer composite does not show a statistically significant improvement (≥10%) in effective thermal conductivity compared to the control, or if it exhibits any notable degradation in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis will be rejected.
